Thermodynamics and the kinetic theory

Chapter 1. The development of ideas about the nature of heat — the basic principles of the kinetic theory · Chapter 1. The development of ideas about the nature of heat — the basic principles of the kinetic theory · Printed page 6

The textbook connects the development of a quantitative theory of thermal processes in the second half of the nineteenth century with the law of energy conservation.
That theory is thermodynamics.

Thermodynamics describes thermal behavior through measurable properties of a system without following each molecule separately.
It is called a phenomenological theory because it relates observable behavior without requiring a detailed microscopic model.
This does not mean that its descriptions are unreliable or that microscopic structure is unimportant.

Thermodynamics uses quantities measured with instruments such as thermometers and pressure gauges.
It describes macroscopic systems rather than the path of each individual molecule.
A macroscopic body contains many particles and can be described by large-scale properties.

Gas in a bottle, water in a glass, a grain of sand, a stone, a steel rod, and Earth are the examples associated with Figure 111.
The objects in the illustration are not drawn to a common physical scale.
For a calculation, we choose a model: a simplified description whose assumptions fit the body and the conditions being studied.

For example, we must ask whether one temperature can adequately describe the body, or whether different parts need different temperatures.
Being a large body does not mean that Earth, a steel rod, or every other example always has one uniform temperature.

Figure 1

Thermal processes often involve energy transfer and conversion.
The system is the body or material chosen for study.
Everything outside it is called the surroundings.

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
Work is another way of transferring energy, for example by pushing, compressing, or stirring.
For a system that exchanges no matter with its surroundings, the first law of thermodynamics says that its change in stored energy equals the net energy transferred to it as heat and work.

The development of energy conservation also helped the particle theory of heat, now called kinetic theory.
Kinetic theory connects large-scale behavior with the motion and interactions of atoms or molecules.
The classical model describes particle motion with Newton's laws, an approximation that works only when its assumptions fit the conditions.

For atoms under conditions where quantum effects matter, this classical model may not give correct predictions.
It is not a complete description of every microscopic process under every possible condition.

By the end of the nineteenth century, theories describing the collective behavior of many atoms and molecules had developed.
The textbook connects kinetic theory with statistical mechanics.
Experimental evidence supports these theories within their ranges of applicability.

Statistical mechanics uses the behavior of many particles to explain large-scale properties;
it is not simply a second name for every particular kinetic model.

Kinetic theory did not make thermodynamics unnecessary.
Thermodynamic laws remain useful for understanding phenomena and calculating the behavior of technical equipment.
They can apply to different materials without first specifying each material's microscopic structure.

This broad usefulness does not remove the conditions required for a particular thermodynamic model or calculation.

A body's heat capacity describes how much energy is needed to raise that body's temperature by one degree under stated conditions, without a change of phase.
This property can be measured experimentally and used in a thermodynamic calculation.
The thermodynamic laws alone do not give every body's heat capacity.

Statistical mechanics can connect such properties with information about microscopic structure and interactions.
Quantitative models of solids and liquids can be complicated.
For many purposes, a simpler thermodynamic calculation using suitable measured properties is therefore valuable.

Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics are complementary.
Thermodynamics relates large-scale properties, while statistical mechanics connects those properties with a microscopic model.
Each explanation depends on whether the model's assumptions fit the body and the conditions being studied.

Statistical mechanics can explain thermodynamic laws when its microscopic model and the system's conditions are suitable.
Neither approach eliminates every limitation or every need for experimental evidence.

We will begin with the basic ideas of kinetic theory.
The original course treats these ideas as a review of material introduced in earlier school years.
